Bellman-Ford handles the negative weight, so the returned path A, D, F is in the accent color. The card reads cost 3 + (−2) = 1." width="100%"} Computes the shortest weighted path from source to target using the Bellman-Ford algorithm. Unlike Dijkstra's algorithm, Bellman-Ford can handle negative edge weights and will detect negative weight cycles. Can return the path as a list, or store the position of each node along the path as a node attribute for visualization. The Bellman-Ford algorithm is slower than Dijkstra (O(VE) vs O(E log V)) but more versatile. Use it when: - the graph has negative edge weights - the graph is sparse, with few edges - you need to detect negative cycles Edge weights are always used, whether or not the graph was created with `weighted=True`; edges without a weight count as `1.0`. In directed graphs, the path follows edge directions. In an undirected graph each edge can be traversed both ways, so a single negative edge that is reachable from `source=` already forms a negative cycle and raises an error; negative weights are therefore only meaningful in directed graphs. Only cycles reachable from `source=` are detected; a negative cycle elsewhere in the graph does not affect the result. If several paths have the same total weight, one of them is returned. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [source]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node where the path starts, given as an integer node ID or a string label. An unknown label raises a `ValueError`; an integer ID that is not in the graph makes the method return `None`. [target]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Node where the path ends, given as an integer node ID or a string label, with the same rules as `source=`. If `target=` equals `source=`, the path is just that node. [attr_name]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the node attribute to store path position. If `None`, uses `bellman_ford_path_order` as the attribute name. Position is 0-indexed (source = 0, next node = 1, ..., target = n-1). Only nodes on the path get this attribute set; all other nodes get a null value. Only used when `return_list=` is `False`. [return_list]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[False]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, returns list of node IDs in the path and leaves the node DataFrame untouched. If `False` (default), stores positions as node attributes under `attr_name=` and returns self for chaining. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Union[list[int], Graph, None]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `return_list=` is `True`: list of node IDs from source to target (inclusive), or `None` if no path exists. If `return_list=` is `False`: returns self for method chaining, or `None` if no path exists. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph contains a negative weight cycle reachable from `source=`, or if `source=` or `target=` is an ID or label that does not exist in the graph. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Bellman-Ford relaxes every edge $V - 1$ times, so it costs $O(V \cdot E)$ time and $O(V)$ space, one factor slower than Dijkstra's $O((V + E) \log V)$. What justifies the extra work is that Bellman-Ford tolerates *negative* edge weights: whenever a shorter path exists that dips below the current distance estimate, the next relaxation round finds it. A final $V$-th pass tries to relax again, and any distance that still decreases proves the existence of a negative-weight cycle, which the implementation surfaces as `ValueError` rather than returning an unbounded path. That negative-cycle detector is what makes Bellman-Ford the standard tool for arbitrage detection in currency graphs, cost-penalty routing where discounts appear as negative weights, and game-theoretic setups with negative payoffs, on top of the plain shortest-path role it plays on graphs with occasional negative edges. ## Examples {.doc-examples} The direct edge from A to B costs `4`, but going through C costs `2 + (-3) = -1`, so the cheapest route to D detours through C and then takes the negative edge to B: ::: {#9652c433 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B", 4.0), ("A", "C", 2.0), ("C", "B", -3.0), # Negative weight ("B", "D", 1.0), ] ) ) path = graph.bellman_ford_shortest_path("A", "D", return_list=True) [graph.get_label_from_id(nid) for nid in path] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` ['A', 'C', 'B', 'D'] ``` ::: ::: With `return_list=False` (the default), each node on the path gets its position as a node attribute, which can feed straight into an aesthetic method for visualization: ::: {#b8f1f93e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} ( graph .bellman_ford_shortest_path("A", "D") .colorize_node_attrs( node_attr_from="bellman_ford_path_order", palette="plasma" ) .get_node_df() .select(["label", "bellman_ford_path_order"]) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: A cycle whose total weight is negative (here `1 - 3 + 1 = -1`) would make paths arbitrarily cheap, so the method raises a `ValueError` instead of returning a path: ::: {#24b5ad6a .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} bad_graph = ( ec.Graph(directed=True) .add_nodes(["A", "B", "C"]) .add_edges( [ ("A", "B", 1.0), ("B", "C", -3.0), ("C", "A", 1.0), # Creates negative cycle ] ) ) error_message = None try: bad_graph.bellman_ford_shortest_path("A", "B", return_list=True) except ValueError as e: error_message = str(e) error_message ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` 'Graph contains a negative weight cycle' ``` ::: ::: If the target cannot be reached, the method returns `None`: ::: {#0913c48b .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph = ec.Graph(directed=True) graph.add_node(label="A") graph.add_node(label="isolated") graph.bellman_ford_shortest_path("A", "isolated", return_list=True) is None ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` True ``` ::: :::
